assessment: The incumbent supplies an assembled, rearrangeable organizer and enabled seven of ten observed customers to reach their ordered arrangement unaided (D2-O4). Its 11-minute median and five reported partition problems indicate unresolved performance, although reports do not establish verified omission rates (D2-O2, D2-O3). D2-O6 limits an account in which assembly is uniformly too slow: repeated three-compartment orders took seven to nine minutes, while every extreme delay occurred in mixed batches. Layout complexity and switching remain confounded. Width overlap in D2-O5 also limits a width-only explanation of insertion retries. No supplied observation establishes the pilot targets or identifies a single dominant cause.

openings.claim: Does changing layout between orders increase selection and checking time independently of compartment count?
openings.delta: Distinguishes a sequencing bottleneck from intrinsically slower complex layouts before changing the assembled product.
openings.prediction: A switching effect predicts longer selection/checking for the same layout immediately after a different layout; a complexity effect predicts longer times by compartment count even in repeated runs.
openings.probe: Using reusable samples within the 15-sample allowance, have both workers perform matched layouts in repeated and interleaved sequences, counterbalancing sequence order and holding exterior color constant. Time selection, insertion, checking and packing separately; record component discrepancies. Limit trials to time compatible with the fixed delivery date.
assumptions: Trial time fits available working time and the initial spending cap.
Practice and fatigue are sufficiently balanced to interpret differences.

openings.claim: An order-specific diagram identifying the short partition and its destination may improve unaided arrangement success.
openings.delta: Targets the observed localization difficulty without removing workshop assembly or partition rearrangeability.
openings.prediction: With independently verified complete kits, the revised diagram produces fewer short-partition placement errors and help requests than the existing three-layout diagram.
openings.probe: Assign the ten willing participants to matched ordered layouts with either diagram; verify contents first and record placement errors, help requests and completion time. Use this small comparison to assess the mechanism, then retain the 60-unit targets for pilot acceptance. Measure diagram preparation time and costs before adoption.
assumptions: Diagram ambiguity contributes to difficulty even when contents are correct.
Revision fits both cost caps and the fixed delivery date while retaining selected compartments, color, footprint and capacity.
